Lexicon Latīnitātis Cotīdiānae

Everyday Latin for conversation, family routines and play with Theo. Long vowels carry macrons; uncertain loanword quantities and our own modern formations are clearly identified.

Macrons, usage and evidence

Macrons mark long vowels; short vowels are left plain. A heavy syllable is not automatically a long vowel. Consonantal i is written j (jam, ejus, conjungō), and the vowel before intervocalic j is left unmarked (major); search treats i and j alike. Inflected examples, genitives, principal parts and Latin headings are included in the review.

For ancient vocabulary, the main references are Lewis & Short and Lewis’s Elementary Latin Dictionary through Perseus and Logeion, with Dickinson’s core list for cross-checking. Hidden quantities are also compared against Bennett’s discussion with Michelson’s corrections and notes on Allen. Dictionary omissions are not automatically proof of shortness; disputed lengths are identified where relevant.

Bulgarian translations accompany the construction, workshop and house-layout vocabulary reviewed on 24 October 2026; search accepts all three languages.

For modern words, the classical lengths of inherited roots and regular Latin endings are retained where justified. Loanword stem quantities that the checked sources do not establish are explicitly labelled. “Reading convention” marks an adopted reconstruction, rather than an attested ancient pronunciation.

Ancient Latin means the word and its relevant basic sense are ancient. Lexicographic evidence means a modern dictionary records the expression; it does not imply universal acceptance. Modern extension applies an older word to a modern object. Working formation identifies our own phrase or name adaptation.

Example sentences are composed for conversation with Theo. They are not quotations unless an author and passage are identified. Noun genitives and genders, important sense distinctions, and known alternative forms are supplied where useful.

Review notes · 24 October 2026

All 53 original grouped entries were reviewed; 39 household and family entries were added. Quantities, examples, definitions and attestation labels were checked separately. The review also removes unsupported precise dates, unsourced principal parts and blanket “attested” tags.

5 October 2026 addition: three family-play entries cover trampoline jumping, Sīmius et arbor and Nauta et undae. The game titles and spoken prompts are our own; modern senses are labelled. The plural genua has short u.

7 October 2026 addition: ausum is the preferred ancient word for “adventure” in the sense of a daring undertaking or venture; adventūra is retained as a medieval/modern alternative, with its semantic development explicitly noted.

11 October 2026 addition: seven workshop-and-repair entries distinguish ancient tool vocabulary from later technical Latin and our own descriptive formations. The review replaces the earlier unsupported cochleārius for “screwdriver” with lexicographically attested vertitōrium, prefers forceps for pliers, records variable vowel quantity in cochlea and terebra, and distinguishes English “dowel” (scalmus) from Bulgarian дюбел. For the latter, ancora mūrālis plastica is explicitly marked as our provisional descriptive formation, not as an attested traditional term.

18 October 2026 addition: 27 grouped entries cover the family smoothie guide: ingredients, equipment, materials, measurements, preparation verbs and phrases for cooking with Theodōrus. Traupman’s uploaded Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, Morgan–Owens and ancient dictionaries were compared. Recorded modern terms, older words with modern senses, uncertain quantities and our composed descriptions are labelled separately. Start with smoothie ingredients · Source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover construction, house layout, furnishings, trowels, a crowbar, extension leads, cable reels and sheet-metal shears. Existing workshop entries were extended with Bulgarian terminology and the recorded tape-measure phrase. Descriptive formations and uncertain ancient senses remain explicit. Construction vocabulary source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover hooks, swinging, pipes, gravel, movement, flips, trenches, dirt, heaps, squeezing/crushing, crashes, missions/quests, caps, scaffolding and its parts/actions. Eight existing entries were extended or cross-linked for rods/bars, blankets, lids, planks, wiping and food-preparation verbs. This batch adds English–Latin vocabulary only. Physical senses, modern applications and our composed descriptions remain distinct. Site and play vocabulary source audit.

25 October 2026: a dedicated Lūdī et lūdibria category adds 14 grouped playground/toy entries and brings the existing swing entry into the same filter. Playground source audit.

Selected quantity corrections
  • ramus / ramulus / ramos → rāmus / rāmulus / rāmōs
  • gravedō / gravedinis → gravēdō / gravēdinis
  • involucrum / manubrium → involūcrum / manūbrium
  • scabī / vesīca / semita → scābī / vēsīca / sēmita
  • vaccinium / morum → vaccīnium / mōrum
  • frīgeō / algēō / fervēō / languēō → frīgeō / algeō / ferveō / langueō
  • elaborātiō / recognitiō → ēlabōrātiō / recōgnitiō
  • program(m)ātum as a noun genitive plural → programmatum; verbal programmātum is a different form
Usage corrections

Ancient fermentō, fermentēscō and vapōrō are no longer called exclusively later inventions. Berry names distinguish modern botanical use from uncertain ancient identification. Totoro, the magnetic-toy phrase and specific Git phrases are labelled as our own adaptations.

The kettle expression and unsupported yogurt or coffee stem quantities are described with their actual level of evidence. Source links appear inside each entry.
